newsitem.title: INDIA: Bombay shares end lower, but cap early losses.
newsitem.headline: Bombay shares end lower, but cap early losses.

text.p: Blue chips at Bombay exchanges on Tuesday crawled higher from the day's lows, with market players pinning hopes on the return of former finance minister P. Chidambaram to the government, dealers said.
Bombay's benchmark 30-share index ended 16.77 points, or 0.44 percent, lower at 3,808.74 provisional close.
"By and large, people are positive. They are expecting some reconciliation," said Neeraj Roy, head of institutional sales at Prime Broking.

G.K. Moopanar, leader of the regional Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) party planned to hold a news conference at 5 p.m. (1130 GMT) to announce whether or not it would join Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's week-old coalition government.
The TMC, the third largest component of the 15-party United Front, quit the government on April 19 after its leader was passed over in the choice of a new leader and prime minister.
Prime Minister Gujral is expected to ask Chidambaram to continue as finance minister and pilot the 1997/98 (April-March) budget through parliament which reconvenes on Wednesday.

Under the budget proposals presented on February 28, Chidambaram -its "main architect", planned wide-ranging cuts in personal and corporate taxes, increased foreign portfolio limit in local firms and legalised buy-back of shares by companies.
"The uncertainty bugging the market should ease off once Chidambaram comes back and ensures the safe passage of the budget," an equites dealer at a domestic brokerage said.
Pressure on the leader of Gujral's Janata Dal Party to quit over a $280 million corruption case cast a shadow on the fledgling minority government, market players said.
Shares of Indo-Gulf Fertilisers ended one rupee, or 3.4 percent, lower at 28.75 at the Bombay exchange after the firm announced a fall in its 1996/97 (April-March) net.
Indo-Gulf's net profit fell 25.4 percent to 1.08 billion rupees during the year ended March 31, 1997 from 1.45 billion.
